Understand the prediction

Could a cyclone first reach 34 knots in this ocean cell during the next 24 hours? This experiment learns from past weather and compares its answers with IMD observations.

Three different questions

Formation

Will a first observed 34-knot crossing happen within 24 hours? This page shows that experiment.

Track and intensity

Where will an existing storm go, and how strong will its winds be? These require separate models and evaluation.

Current footprint

Which locations are inside a defined wind or cloud boundary now? Formation scores do not answer this.

Why these data?

ERA5 weather: what the model sees

Sea-surface temperature, mean sea-level pressure, 10 m east/west and north/south wind, 2 m temperature and dewpoint. Spatial summaries describe ocean warmth, pressure, near-surface flow and moisture. Upper-air wind shear and humidity are deferred until matching coverage is complete.

Open Abhishek Bisht’s ERA5 folder
IBTrACS / IMD: how the answer is checked

Observed storm positions, NEWDELHI grades and winds supply the labels. Unknown observations are excluded from affected cell windows. They are not automatically counted as “no formation.” A first threshold crossing requires an earlier observed subthreshold wind.

Why GFS cannot replace ERA5 directly

The model’s numerical rules were fitted to ERA5 fields. A different weather model can shift their distributions. The research inference helper rejects a GFS source; live GFS forecasts need their own validation or a tested adaptation.

What the paper contributes

The supplied PLOS paper studies satellite-image cyclone classification and intensity estimation. It helps separate current-state tasks from future formation. Its published accuracy is not the accuracy of this experiment. INSAT fusion has not been trained here.
